h1: Labour Hutments: Single-Room Units from 10x10 Feet
seoTitle: Labour Hutments Price List, 6 Sizes and Layouts | SAMAN
metaDescription: Labour hutments in six sizes from 10x10 to 20x20 ft, sleeping 4 to 16 workers. Compare prices, wall options and room layouts, then request a site quote.
opener: A labour hutment is one small sleeping unit, built complete in the factory and set down on its own plinth. SAMAN makes it in six sizes, from 10x10 ft for four workers to 20x20 ft for sixteen, so a site can add beds in the quantity it actually needs instead of committing to a full colony block. The frame is welded and bolted mild steel to IS 2062 or approved equivalent. Walls are a choice of profiled GI sheet or 30 to 40 mm insulated PUF panel. Every unit carries one 900 mm class door, two opposing sliding windows for cross ventilation, fan and light points and a labelled distribution board. Bunks, lockers, sanitation and the civil base are quoted separately, so the published price is the shell you receive.
descriptionHtml:
What a labour hutment actually is

A labour hutment is a single prefabricated room, built in the factory and delivered as one piece, in which workers sleep. That is the whole of it. It is not a building with corridors, it is not a block with a staircase, and it is not a camp with its own kitchen. Understanding that boundary is the fastest way to work out whether a hutment is what your site needs, because most of the confusion in this market comes from the word being used loosely for anything temporary that a workforce sleeps in.

The unit arrives complete: frame, walls, roof, floor, door, windows, lights, fan points and a distribution board. It is set down on prepared plinth pads and connected to the site's power supply. Workers can occupy it the same week. Nothing about it needs a foundation crew, a mason or a wet trade on site.

Where it sits between a shed and a colony

Three products in the SAMAN Labour Colony range solve three different problems, and picking the wrong one costs money.

A labour shed is one large open enclosure. Everybody sleeps in a single space. It is cheaper per bed at scale and quicker to erect over a big footprint, and it suits a workforce that is uniform, single shift and temporary. If that describes your requirement, the labour shed range is the honest recommendation and this page is not.

A labour colony is a planned settlement: several accommodation blocks plus sanitation, a canteen, an admin office, circulation roads and services, designed together. That is a project, not a purchase, and it is priced and planned as one.

A hutment is the unit in between. One room, one door, four to sixteen beds, standing on its own. You buy one, or four, or eleven, and you place them where the site allows. The reason contractors choose it is granularity. A colony has to be committed to in advance; hutments can be added in the quantity the programme actually turns out to need.

Choosing between GI sheet and PUF panel

This is the only material decision most buyers have to make, and it is worth taking seriously because it is the difference between a hutment people can sleep in through a Rajasthan May and one they cannot.

The budget tier uses profiled GI or PPGI steel sheet with bracing and a liner as specified. It is durable, it is cheap, it is easy to repair with materials available anywhere, and it carries no insulation. In a temperate site, at moderate altitude, or where occupancy is short and seasonal, it is entirely adequate.

The insulated tier uses a nominal 30 to 40 mm PUF sandwich panel. The 40 to 60 mm range is available but is only supplied where the signed bill of materials selects it, so it is not something to assume. The panel changes how the room behaves through the afternoon and overnight, particularly under an uninsulated roof.

Two honest qualifications. First, panel thickness on its own is not a thermal performance figure, and this page does not publish one. The behaviour of the room depends on the joints, the roof, the floor, the openings and the site, not on a single number from a brochure. Second, an uninsulated roof over an insulated wall is a common and expensive mistake. If the site is hot, the roof needs either an insulated panel or an approved radiant or ceiling treatment, and that is priced separately.

How the room is planned

The internal arrangement is deliberately plain, and every element in it earns its place.

Beds and aisle. Bunks stand against the long walls with a clear aisle down the centre. The published occupancy for each size assumes that arrangement. Crowding beds into the aisle raises the headline number and destroys the thing that makes the room usable at three in the morning when someone is coming off shift.

Lockers. Lockable personal storage is what turns shared accommodation from a dormitory into something people will look after. Lockers are itemised separately from the shell price, and it is worth ordering them with the unit rather than later.

Two-room option. From 180 sq ft upward the module can be split into two simple sleeping rooms, each with its own door. Sites use this to house a supervisor separately, or to accommodate a couple, without ordering a second unit.

Cross ventilation, and why the windows face each other

Each hutment carries two openable aluminium sliding windows, and they sit on opposite walls rather than side by side. That is not a styling decision. Air has to enter at one end of the room and leave at the other for the draught to reach the beds in the middle. Two windows on the same wall ventilate the wall, not the room.

Window sill height and bed position are coordinated so a bunk does not stand across an opening and block the airflow the room depends on. Removable mosquito mesh, louvres, privacy screens and protected MS grilles are all available as options, but they are options, and where an opening forms part of the escape strategy a fixed grille must not compromise it.

Ceiling or wall fans are provided as fixed points. A split-AC point is fitted only when it is specifically ordered. The baseline unit is designed around natural ventilation and fans, not sealed mechanical cooling, and a hot or humid site should expect to move to the insulated tier or add cooling after a load review rather than assume it.

Structure, floor and relocation

The frame is welded and bolted mild steel, using IS 2062 or IS 1161 class structural steel or approved equivalent. Member sizes, weld sizes, bolt grades and joint details come from the fabrication drawings for the specific order, not from any nominal schedule, and IS 800 and the project welding requirements are design references rather than a certification.

Two floor options exist and they lead to different products.

The prefab floor uses steel joists carrying an 18 to 24 mm cement, cement-fibre or plywood class board with a vinyl finish. This is the option to specify if the unit may be lifted and relocated. Board edges are supported and sealed, and the assembly is built for sweeping and mopping around beds rather than for wet use.

The fixed floor is a level RCC plinth with screed. It is the better option where the unit will stay put for its whole life, and it removes the joist depth from the step-up at the door.

Relocation deserves a plain warning. A single-piece-lift model and a dismantlable panel model use different connections and different lifting details, and they are identified separately at order stage. Lifting lugs, corner fittings and skid points appear only where the signed general arrangement and lifting drawing show them. A lift plan needs the finished weight, the centre of gravity, the sling geometry and the support points, and forklift handling is permitted only where the pockets and the capacity are documented. Do not assume a unit can be picked up in one piece because a similar one could.

Electrical scope, and what is not in it

Wiring is FR or FRLS copper in approved conduit or trunking, with protected metal penetrations and separation from water, waste and flexible module joints. Typical references are 1.5 sq mm for lighting, 2.5 sq mm for socket circuits and 4 sq mm for air-conditioning or other high-load circuits, but the final cable size is confirmed by the project electrical schedule against the connected load, the voltage drop and the protection coordination. The steel frame and exposed conductive parts are bonded to the tested site earth.

Protection comprises a main isolator, MCB, RCBO or RCCB protection as the design requires, labelled neutral and earth bars, bonding, and surge protection where the supply or the risk assessment calls for it. Wet-area circuits, generator or DG changeover, fault level and the external supply interface all follow the approved single-line diagram. SAMAN supplies and installs to that design; the workbook does not certify the site installation, and the final connection and testing remain a site responsibility.

Fixed lights, fan points, 6A and 16A sockets and exhaust points are provided in the quantities on the approved room and electrical schedule. Loose appliances, air-conditioning units, UPS and data equipment are excluded unless they are itemised.

Sanitation is a separate building

The baseline sleeping hutment has no internal plumbing. There is no attached toilet, no shower and no washbasin unless a basin or pantry point is specifically ordered with its own dedicated supply and waste connection.

This is a deliberate scope boundary, not an omission. Keeping wet services out of the sleeping unit keeps the floor build simple, keeps the cost honest and avoids the hidden drainage work that turns a straightforward order into a civil job. Workers use a separate sanitation or ablution block. If the order does include an attached wet module, the floor changes to a waterproof, sloped, drained wet-area system, and that is a different specification and a different price.

Included, optional and excluded

Included in the published price: the steel frame, walls, roof, floor, one personnel door, two windows, internal lining, fixed lights and fan points, sockets and exhaust points to the approved schedule, the distribution board and protection, the coating system, and factory quality checks with handover documentation.

Optional, priced separately: insulated wall or roof upgrade, ceiling, the two-room split, mosquito mesh, louvres, privacy screens, grilles, a split-AC point, a basin or pantry point, and slip-resistant flooring.

Excluded unless scheduled: bunks and mattresses, lockers, attached toilets, external sanitation, air-conditioning equipment, the civil base and plinth, transport, unloading, site electrical supply, statutory approvals, roads, drainage and every other site infrastructure item.

Site readiness before delivery

The unit arrives complete, but the site has to be ready for it. Before the delivery date, confirm a level, compacted and drained standing area; the plinth pads or plinth beam at the correct levels; clear vehicle access for a trailer and, where a crane is being used, for the crane; an electrical supply point within reach; and a decision on where the drainage apron and the external light point go.

None of that is difficult, but all of it takes longer to arrange than people expect, and a unit that arrives before its base is ready has to be stored somewhere.

Ordering, lead time and what we need from you

Delivery is 7 to 21 working days from a confirmed order, and a fixed-price quotation is issued within 48 hours of a complete enquiry. To price accurately we need the selected size or custom dimensions, the quantity, the wall tier, the delivery location, the required delivery sequence, whether the unit must be relocatable, and whether bunks and lockers are in scope.

SAMAN POS India Private Limited manufactures at Bengaluru and Greater Noida. We are a manufacturer, not a reseller, with over 15 years in prefabricated buildings, more than 500 projects and over 3,000 customers across 15 states.

Warranty is stated identically on every SAMAN product: 5-year structural warranty and 1-year finishing warranty as standard; finishing warranty extendable to 2 years on request, confirmed at quotation. Warranty scope and exclusions are confirmed in the final quotation, and misuse, site services, consumables and unapproved alterations remain outside the agreed scope unless explicitly included.

Maintenance and service life

Design life is 20 to 25 years under proper use and maintenance. That is a design life, not a warranty period, and the difference matters.

What shortens it is predictable: blocked roof drainage, damaged coating at cut edges left unrepaired, sealant failures at penetrations, and relocation damage on units that were moved without a lift plan. Inspect the roof fall and flashing before each monsoon, repair coating damage when it appears rather than at handover, and keep the drainage apron clear.

Labour hutment FAQs

How many workers fit in one hutment?

Between four and sixteen depending on the size, and each size on this page publishes its own figure. The number assumes bunks along the walls with a clear central aisle.

Is there a toilet inside?

No. The baseline sleeping hutment has no internal plumbing. Sanitation is a separate block. An attached wet module can be quoted, but it changes the floor specification.

Can the unit be moved to another site later?

Yes, if it is ordered with the prefab floor and the relocation provisions. Specify that at order stage, because a single-piece-lift unit and a dismantlable panel unit are built differently.

What is the difference between a hutment and a labour shed?

A hutment is one small room for a small crew. A shed is one large open enclosure for a bigger workforce in a single space.

Do I need a concrete foundation?

No. Plinth pads or a plinth beam on level, compacted, drained ground are sufficient for the prefab option. An RCC plinth is used where the unit will stay in place permanently.
